841.title: Thomas More and Erasmus
841.hook: two friends, a book called Utopia, and humor with holiness
841.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Thomas More, with Saint John Fisher, on a shared feast in June; he is the patron of statesmen and politicians, and some lawyers' guilds take his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juan Diego, carrying flowers in his cloak to a bishop who doubted him. Your line was the little one. What did you do that felt too big for you? Day eight hundred forty-one.

A scholar is riding on horseback, the long way back from Italy to England, with hours to fill. Rather than waste them, he starts composing a joke in his head: a whole book spoken by Folly herself, a lady who praises fools and mocks the wise. He's on his way to stay with a friend in London, and the friend's name gives him the title. The scholar is Erasmus. The friend is Thomas More. Today's word is the two of them together.
screen: `A LONG RIDE FROM ITALY.` → `A BOOK SPOKEN BY FOLLY.` → `A FRIEND IN LONDON.`

segments.voice: Start with the pun. Erasmus wrote his book in Latin and gave it a Greek title, Moriae Encomium, the Praise of Folly. In his letter to More at the front of it, he explains: moria is the Greek word for folly, and it sounds like More's name. Then he adds that his friend is as far from folly as his name is close to it. A joke between friends, printed in a book. Next, the friend. Erasmus once wrote a long letter describing More for someone who had never met him. He paints a man whose face leans toward cheerfulness, who loved a good joke from boyhood, who could find something to enjoy in almost anyone, and who was at the same time serious about prayer and generous to the poor. Then, More's own book, Utopia. It describes an island where a traveler claims everything is run differently: property shared, gold despised, worship tolerant. The name is a made-up word, and the book itself plays games with it. Readers still argue about how much of it More meant and how much was a joke with a sting in it. That uncertainty is part of the fun. Finally, why it matters for holiness. More is a canonized saint. The stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end. Wit, for him, didn't compete with faith. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh." These two friends seem to have taken both halves of that line seriously.
screen: `MORIA, AND MORE.` · `A FACE THAT LEANS TOWARD CHEER.` · `AN ISLAND CALLED UTOPIA.` · `A SAINT WHO KEPT JOKING.` · then, large: `A TIME TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember laughing with a friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one friend you've laughed with until you couldn't stop. Find the moment: where you were, what set it off, their face. Let a smile come if it wants to. If you pray, you can give thanks for that friend, by name. If you don't, just stay with the memory and let it warm the room. Then, after the bell, if you can, send that friend one line that might make them laugh. The bell holds the time.
Utopia. Thomas More's book about an island run differently, written while trading jokes in Latin with his friend Erasmus. Today's word.
Your line: witty and holy. Today, make one person laugh on purpose, kindly, and notice whether it cost your seriousness anything. Day eight hundred forty-one.

pairs: a time to weep, and a time to laugh

842.title: Erasmus
842.hook: a scholar who wanted reform by learning and gentleness
842.howItsDone: Erasmus is not a canonized saint and has no feast day; Catholics and Protestants alike read his editions, letters and satires as part of the history of reform, and scholars still argue over how to place him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Utopia, written by Thomas More while trading jokes in Latin with Erasmus. Your line was witty and holy. Who did you make laugh? Day eight hundred forty-two.

A farmer behind a plow, singing to himself as he works. A weaver at the loom, humming in time with the shuttle. A traveler on a long road, passing the miles with a story. Erasmus wrote that picture into the front of a book, and the songs he wanted them singing were the words of the Gospel, from their own memory, in their own tongue. Today's word is the scholar who dreamed it: Erasmus.
screen: `A FARMER SINGING AT THE PLOW.` → `A WEAVER HUMMING AT THE LOOM.` → `THE GOSPEL IN THEIR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Erasmus worked from old Greek manuscripts of the New Testament and published the Greek text with his own Latin translation beside it, so readers could check the Latin against the language the apostles wrote in. That was his kind of reform: go back to the sources and read them carefully. Second, the preface. He called it the Paraclesis, an exhortation, and in it he paints that farmer and weaver and traveler. He wished the Gospels and Paul's letters were in every language, so that ordinary people could know them by heart. Third, the gentleness. Erasmus saw plenty wrong in the Church of his day, and said so, often with jokes. But when Martin Luther broke with Rome, Erasmus did not follow him. He stayed Catholic, and when he finally disagreed with Luther in print, about whether the human will is free, he called his book a discussion, not an attack. Luther answered sharply, in a book of his own. Fourth, the hope underneath it all. Paul writes to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "And be not conformed to this world; but be reformed in the newness of your mind." Erasmus seems to have taken that line at its word. Change the mind, by giving it the text. Reform would come through learning, through reading, through patience, rather than through anger. Whether it can always work that way is still an open question. But he spent his life betting that it could.
screen: `GREEK AND LATIN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE PARACLESIS: SCRIPTURE FOR ALL.` · `HE STAYED, AND DISAGREED GENTLY.` · `REFORMED IN THE NEWNESS OF YOUR MIND.` · then, large: `REFORM BY LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reform one thing gently. Sit, and breathe. Choose one thing you want to change: a habit, a rule at work, a way your family talks to each other. Now, instead of planning a fight, ask what someone would need to understand for it to change. What would they need to read, or hear, or see? Picture saying it calmly, once, with patience. If you pray, you can offer that change to God. If you don't, simply hold the gentler plan in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Erasmus. The scholar who printed the New Testament in Greek beside his own Latin, wanted scripture in every language, and hoped the Church would be reformed by learning. Today's word.
Your line: reform by learning. Today, before you argue with someone, read or ask one thing that helps you understand them better. Day eight hundred forty-two.

843.title: John Fisher (1535)
843.hook: the only bishop who refused Henry VIII, executed two weeks before More
843.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saints John Fisher and Thomas More together in June; in England and Wales, churches, schools and colleges carry their names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Erasmus, the scholar who wanted farmers singing the Gospel at the plow. Your line was reform by learning. What did you try to understand before you argued? Day eight hundred forty-three.

A thin old man is woken early in a cell in the Tower of London and told that today he will die. The story told by his early biographer is that he asked to sleep a little longer, and slept. When he rose, he put on his best clothes, and when someone asked why, he said it was his wedding day. He was a bishop, and a cardinal, and he had said no to the King of England. Today's word is his name: John Fisher.
screen: `WOKEN IN THE TOWER.` → `HIS BEST CLOTHES.` → `A BISHOP WHO SAID NO.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. John Fisher was bishop of Rochester, and he had been a leader of the university of Cambridge, where he welcomed new learning. He brought Erasmus to teach there. He was a scholar and a preacher, known for living plainly. Second, the question. King Henry the Eighth wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon ended, and then wanted to be named head of the Church in England. Fisher defended the queen's marriage openly. When the bishops were asked to swear an oath accepting the king's new claims, Catholic memory holds Fisher up as the bishop who would not take it. He was sent to the Tower. Third, the hat. While he was in prison, Pope Paul the Third named him a cardinal. Tradition says the king, hearing of it, swore that Fisher would wear the hat on his shoulders, because he would leave him no head to set it on. Fourth, the last walk. On the way out to the scaffold, the story goes, Fisher opened his New Testament and asked for a word to carry with him. It fell open at John's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent." He closed the book and said that was learning enough to last him to his life's end. Thomas More followed him to the same death shortly after. Behind both stands a short line from the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles were told to stop preaching: "We ought to obey God, rather than men."
screen: `A SCHOLAR-BISHOP OF ROCHESTER.` · `THE OATH HE WOULD NOT TAKE.` · `THE HEAD AND THE HAT.` · `A WORD FOR THE LAST WALK.` · then, large: `OBEY GOD, RATHER THAN MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold in mind leaders who must say no. Settle, and breathe. Think of bishops and pastors today, and of anyone in charge who is being pushed to bend: a judge, a manager, a teacher, a parent. Choose one. If you pray, you can pray for courageous bishops, and for that one person, that they find the steadiness Fisher found. If you don't, simply wish them courage, and notice what it would cost them to stand still. The bell holds the time.
John Fisher. Bishop of Rochester and cardinal, who refused King Henry's oath, opened his New Testament on the way to the scaffold, and died for it. Today's word.
Your line: the one who refused. Today, if you're asked to go along with something you think is wrong, even something small, say a quiet, clear no. Day eight hundred forty-three.

844.title: The monasteries dissolved
844.hook: England's monasteries closed and stripped in the 1530s
844.howItsDone: Catholics in England remember the martyrs of the dissolution, among them the Carthusians of London and the abbots of Glastonbury, Reading and Colchester; some parishes hold Masses and pilgrimages at old abbey ruins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Fisher, the bishop who said no to the king and opened his New Testament on the way to die. Your line was the one who refused. Where did you say a quiet no? Day eight hundred forty-four.

In a green valley in Yorkshire, tall stone arches stand with no roof on them. Grass grows where the floor of the church used to be. Sheep wander through the doorways. Birds nest in the window frames where the glass was. Visitors walk through with tickets and guidebooks, and on a quiet afternoon the only singing is the wind. These were abbeys, full of people who prayed together every day. Today's word is the king's name: Henry.
screen: `ARCHES WITH NO ROOF.` → `SHEEP IN THE DOORWAYS.` → `ONCE, A HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: First, what a monastery was. A community of monks or nuns who rose in the night and through the day to sing the psalms in choir. Around that prayer grew everything else: schools, libraries, farms, alms at the gate for the poor, a bed for travelers, care for the sick. Second, what the king did. In the years around Fisher's death, Henry the Eighth's officials visited the religious houses, wrote reports against them, and closed them, the smaller ones first and then the great abbeys. Lead was stripped from the roofs and melted down. Bells were taken. Libraries were scattered. The lands were sold or given to men the king wanted to reward. Monks and nuns were turned out, some with pensions. Some abbots who would not surrender were put to death, among them the abbot of Glastonbury. In the north, people rose up in a protest called the Pilgrimage of Grace, partly to defend their abbeys. It was put down. Third, the line. Later, Shakespeare wrote a sonnet about growing old, and pictured bare branches as "Bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang." Some readers hear the empty abbeys in it, the singing gone from the stone. Fourth, the older lament. The book of Lamentations, mourning a ruined Jerusalem, begins in the Douay-Rheims: "How doth the city sit solitary that was full of people!" Those ruins in the valleys still stand. Some people go to them simply to look. Some go to pray where prayer used to be sung.
screen: `PRAYER, AND ALL THAT GREW AROUND IT.` · `ROOFS STRIPPED, BELLS TAKEN.` · `A SONNET'S BARE BRANCHES.` · `SOLITARY, THAT WAS FULL OF PEOPLE.` · then, large: `BARE RUINED CHOIRS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in an empty place. If there's an empty church or an old ruin near you, save a visit there for another day. For now, sit wherever you are and let it be quiet. Bring to mind a church with no roof, grass on the floor, and the sky where the ceiling was. Hear, in your mind, the voices that once sang there, and the silence now. If you pray, you can pray there in your mind, adding your voice where theirs used to be. If you don't, simply listen to the quiet, and to what it holds. The bell holds the time.
Henry. The king whose officials closed England's religious houses, stripped their roofs, and sent their monks and nuns away. Today's word.
Your line: bare ruined choirs. Today, when you pass an empty building, a closed church, or a quiet room, pause for one breath and remember who used to be there. Day eight hundred forty-four.

845.title: Holiness and failure together
845.hook: the middle ages had both inquisitions and hospitals, crusades and Francis
845.howItsDone: Catholics confess sins personally in the sacrament of reconciliation, and the Church has also made public acts of repentance for wrongs done by its members in the past, while continuing to honor the saints of the same centuries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henry, whose officials stripped the monasteries' roofs and left their choirs quiet. Your line was bare ruined choirs. Who did you remember in an empty place? Day eight hundred forty-five.

A farmer's servants come to him with bad news. An enemy has sown weeds in the wheat field while everyone slept, and now the two are coming up together. Shall we go and pull them out? No, says the farmer. You'll tear up the wheat with them. Let both grow until the harvest. Jesus tells that story in Matthew's Gospel. Today, near the end of this long walk through the middle ages, it turns out to be a useful way of looking back. Today's word: cockle.
screen: `WEEDS IN THE WHEAT.` → `SHALL WE PULL THEM OUT?` → `LET BOTH GROW.`

segments.voice: First, the failure, said plainly. The centuries we've walked through had crusades, with massacres along the way. They had inquisitions, courts that questioned and punished people for their beliefs. They had Jews blamed and killed in times of plague, popes who schemed for money and power, and a king who emptied the monasteries. None of that needs softening. Second, the holiness, in the same years. The Rule of Saint Benedict tells monks that care for the sick comes before everything, and that they are to be served as Christ himself. Elizabeth of Hungary founded a hospital and nursed the sick in it. Francis walked unarmed into the camp of a sultan in the middle of a crusade. Julian of Norwich heard that all shall be well. Third, the temptation. It's easy to keep only one list. Some tell the story of these centuries as nothing but darkness. Others tell it as a golden age. Both versions are easier to carry than the truth. Fourth, how the Church describes itself. We heard it with the Renaissance popes: the Second Vatican Council calls the Church at once holy and always in need of being purified. Set that line beside the parable, and it looks a lot like the farmer's field. The Douay-Rheims calls the weeds cockle. The servants want a clean field now. The farmer says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." It isn't permission to excuse the weeds. In the story, the harvest still comes, and the weeds are still weeds. It's a warning against pretending that only one of them ever grew.
screen: `THE FAILURE, SAID PLAINLY.` · `THE HOLINESS, IN THE SAME YEARS.` · `THE TEMPTATION OF ONE LIST.` · `HOLY, AND ALWAYS BEING PURIFIED.` · then, large: `SUFFER BOTH TO GROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both in one thought. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you belong to: a family, a church, a country, a team. Name to yourself one real failure in it, without excuses. Then, without letting go of the first, name one real goodness in it. Keep both in view at once, the way the farmer kept the whole field. If you pray, you can offer both to God together. If you don't, simply hold them side by side until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Cockle. The Douay-Rheims word for the weeds in Jesus's parable, left to grow beside the wheat until harvest, the way holiness and failure grew together in the medieval Church. Today's word.
Your line: both are true. Today, when someone describes a person or a group as all good or all bad, quietly add the other half in your head. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: Medieval close: a mirror
846.hook: every age of saints shows what that age most needed
846.howItsDone: Catholics read the lives of the saints through the year, keeping their feasts in the Church's calendar; homilies and spiritual reading often ask what a saint's life says to the present day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cockle, the weeds that grew beside the wheat in one field. Your line was both are true. Where did you add the other half? Today closes the middle ages. Day eight hundred forty-six.

Hold up a mirror to a room and it shows you the room. Not an idea of it. What's actually there, including what's missing: the empty chair, the bare wall. For a long stretch now we've walked through the middle ages, from a monastery bell to a stripped abbey roof. Today we hold up a mirror to the whole stretch, and the mirror is the saints. Today's word: mirror.
screen: `A MIRROR SHOWS THE ROOM.` → `INCLUDING WHAT'S MISSING.` → `THE SAINTS AS A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Here's one way to read them: each age's saints show what that age was short of. First, violence. In an age of private wars and crusades, we met the Peace of God, Louis the king doing justice under an oak, and Francis walking unarmed to a sultan. Peace was what was missing, so peacemakers shone. Second, ignorance and confusion. The universities rose, Thomas the dumb ox reasoned his way toward God, and Bonaventure mapped a journey of the mind. When the popes lived away from Rome, a dyer's daughter, Catherine, told one to go home. Third, suffering. When plague came, Julian, walled in beside her church, heard that all shall be well, and saw all that is made, as small as a hazelnut in her hand. Elizabeth and Catherine of Genoa nursed the sick. Fourth, power and greed. When popes grew worldly and empires reached for gold, Las Casas changed, a pope wrote that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, Juan Diego the little one carried flowers to a bishop, and Fisher refused a king. Mirrors don't flatter. Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Looking back, we see these centuries through a glass too: partly, darkly, with our own reflection in the frame. And Jesus once told some questioners who could read the sky that they could not read "the signs of the times." That's the harder question this block leaves behind. Not what did their age need. What does ours?
screen: `AN AGE OF VIOLENCE: PEACEMAKERS.` · `AN AGE OF CONFUSION: TEACHERS.` · `AN AGE OF PLAGUE: HEALERS.` · `AN AGE OF GREED: THOSE WHO CHANGED.` · then, large: `THE SIGNS OF THE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what your age needs. Sit, and breathe. Look around your own time the way we've looked at theirs: your city, your news, your group chats, your family. Ask quietly, what is missing here? What kind of person would shine, simply by being the opposite of what's wrong? Don't rush to an answer. Let one come. If you pray, you can ask to be shown it. If you don't, just keep the question open until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mirror. The image for this look back at the middle ages, where the saints show what each age was missing, and now ask what ours is short of. Today's word.

Your line: what does my age need. Today, ask it once of someone you trust, and listen to their answer before giving yours. Tomorrow a new block begins, reform, mission and revolution, with a soldier hit by a cannonball. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Pamplona, 1521
847.hook: a cannonball smashes a soldier's leg, and bored in bed he reads the lives of saints
847.howItsDone: Some Catholics keep a book of saints' lives or read about the saint of the day, and Ignatius's own account of his conversion is read in Jesuit schools and on retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the middle ages with a mirror: every age of saints shows what that age needed. Your line was what does my age need. Did an answer come? This week walked from More and Erasmus to holiness and failure side by side. Today a new block opens: reform, mission and revolution. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

A fortress wall, a French army outside it, and a young Basque officer who won't surrender. The others want to surrender. He talks the commander into fighting. Then a cannonball comes through, and it shatters one of his legs and wounds the other. The fortress falls. The French, impressed, carry him home on a litter. He is Íñigo López de Loyola, a courtier who loved fine clothes, sword fights and stories of knights. The world will know him as Ignatius. And the place where his first life ended has a name: Pamplona.
screen: `A FORTRESS THAT WON'T SURRENDER.` → `A CANNONBALL.` → `CARRIED HOME ON A LITTER.`

segments.voice: Ignatius told this story himself, near the end of his life, to a younger Jesuit who wrote it down. He tells it about himself in the third person, and he isn't kind to his younger self. First, vanity. The leg was set badly, and a bone stuck out below the knee. He couldn't bear how it would look in a knight's tight boots, so he had the bone cut away and the leg stretched, by his own choice, and bore the pain without a word. That's the man in the bed: proud, brave, and bored. Second, the books. He asked for the romances of chivalry he loved. There were none in the house. What they had was a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. So he read those, because there was nothing else. Third, the daydreams. He found himself imagining what it would be like to do what Saint Francis did, what Saint Dominic did. If they could do it, why not him? Then his mind would drift back to a noble lady and the deeds he'd do for her. He noticed something about how each daydream left him afterward, and that noticing would shape his whole life. Fourth, the turn. Nothing outside him had planned this. A war, a wound, an empty bookshelf. Some readers hold a life like this up to a line from Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "to them that love God, all things work together unto good." Not that the cannonball was good. Ignatius limped for the rest of his life. But the cannonball is where his story started.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one saint's life, or a piece of one. Settle, and breathe. If you have a book or a phone nearby, find a few lines about any saint and read them slowly. If not, bring to mind one you already know. Don't study. Just notice what catches, the way Ignatius did. One thing they did. Then ask, lightly: what would that look like in my life, this week? If you pray, you can ask that saint to pray for you. If you don't, simply hold their story for a while. The bell holds the time.
Pamplona. The fortress town where a cannonball broke a soldier's leg, and a sickbed with nothing to read but saints began the life of Ignatius of Loyola.
Your line: the cannonball. Today, when something interrupts your plans, pause before you push it away and ask what's sitting on the shelf in the room it put you in. Day eight hundred forty-seven.
